  • First with one model, sixteenth with another

    Nov 17, 2026

    Runta and Baseten ran 27,280 agent trials — 22 harness configurations across 5 open models — and measured what harness leaderboards were hiding: with the model fixed, the harness moves cost per task 1.8 to 5.0x, and the most expensive harness per pass usually passed less often than the cheapest. The same shape runs through accuracy: Wiz's arena shows a 5.1-point mean gap for the same models across two harnesses, and ARC-AGI-3's Standard-versus-Provider-Adapter pairs sit 18 to 45 points apart at matched effort. Steps per pass predicts the bill; prompt size does not. Publish the pairing, not just the model.

  • What a remembered yes remembers

    Nov 16, 2026

    An AppleScript yes minted in one session later vouched for a write to the policy file it had nothing to do with, reproduced red and fixed green on an open upstream branch. The same widened row shows up as an allow-list entry with no record of the image it was minted for, a 503 with no receipt retried blind, and a plan approved unread. What a remembered yes has to carry to stay a consent record: the bytes, the evidence, the boundary, and a per-property answer about what resets and what persists across a restart.

  • No one repaired the fallback

    Nov 15, 2026

    CrewAI's code interpreter answered "what runs when Docker is unreachable" by executing the code in the tool process itself: a probe against 1.10.1 came back uid=1003 with the runner's own pid and ctypes loadable, while the same probe in the container returned uid=0 pid=7. Release 1.13.0 refused instead, and the tool was then deleted outright. This week, plimsoll 0.27.1 and Microsoft's MXC 1.1.0 answered the same question the same way: refuse before code is sent, or remove the path.

Notes — short finds

  • Nov 18, 2026

    An agent edits a config file. You fix another line yourself, then reopen the conversation to see what the agent changed. The file at that path now contains both edits. On a different machine the file might not be there at all.

    Docker Agent 1.162.0 still reads the file to show a preview before you approve an edit. Once the edit has run, the terminal UI draws the diff from the tool’s saved result instead. The renderer test, which I read but didn’t run, reloads the result from JSON, then overwrites and deletes the file. It clears the render cache after each change and checks that the old diff still looks the same.

    A formatter failure makes the distinction useful. The tool writes the file before running a configured post-edit command, so the session can show an error even though the file changed. When the tool can record the final contents, the expanded view can put the diff next to the error. Old results without recorded diffs get no reconstructed patch. When I pick up a coding session again, I want the old diff to tell me what the tool changed and a fresh read to tell me what I’d be editing now.

  • Nov 18, 2026

    A coding agent changes a schema, runs the build, and opens the generated file to check its work. The build succeeds. The file still describes the old schema.

    I tried a version small enough to fit in a Make rule. With accent in base.txt and blue in schema.txt, this makes accent=blue:

    out.txt: base.txt
	printf '%s=%s\n' "$$(cat base.txt)" "$$(cat schema.txt)" > $@

    I changed the schema to gold. Make left accent=blue alone. Deleting the output and building afresh gave accent=gold, as did declaring schema.txt after base.txt and repeating the edit.

    Google’s ABFS design describes what to do when a build graph has a lot of gaps like this. Its Ninja executor uses the declared inputs, command and relevant environment to find candidate results, then checks the files and directories recorded from the earlier run before restoring an output. I tried that second check in a small Python cache, without running ABFS. The declared key stayed the same after the schema edit. Without checking the recorded reads I got blue back; with the check the cache rejected blue and rebuilt gold. Editing an unrelated file still gave me a hit. Changing an environment value left out of my toy key gave me the wrong hit again: the file reads agreed because the changed input wasn’t a file.

    For a coding agent’s tool cache, I’d change one file the command read but the request didn’t name, then compare the returned bytes with a clean run. I’d also change a file the command never touched and make sure reuse still works. A cache that always reruns would pass the first test.

  • Nov 18, 2026

    Slack gets the incident report. The second destination refuses it, so the worker retries. Now Slack can get the same report twice, even though it was the destination that worked.

    Sergey Kamardin calls out that trade-off in Pagedog. The investigation worker saves the report, then Spooler acknowledges the incident and queues the report reference together. The server’s notification loop tries every destination and acknowledges the report only when they all succeed. A partial failure can bring the whole report back for another try. Pagedog buys simpler bookkeeping at the price of possible duplicate notifications.

    I tried the notification step with two fake destinations and separate SQLite files for queue state and deliveries, rather than running Pagedog. After A succeeded and B refused, retrying the whole report left two deliveries at A and one at B. Saving A’s receipt before moving on kept it to one each. Then I stopped the worker just after A returned success, before it could save the receipt. On restart A got two copies again. When I made the receiver enforce a unique key for each report and destination, both failures ended with one delivery at each. The queue showed the report acknowledged after replay in every case.

    I’d keep the sender’s receipts so a flaky destination doesn’t make the others do extra work. Where a receiver supports idempotency, I’d also reuse the same delivery key on retry. The test I’d keep is the awkward one: interrupt the worker after the receiver commits and before the sender records it, then count what’s at each destination.

  • Nov 17, 2026

    On a Windows machine, plimsoll versions 0.27.0 and 0.27.1 answered a request for VM-grade isolation with a yes whenever the daemon ran the WSL containers provider. The yes was a tier label, vm, the strongest of the four walls plimsoll reports, and every floor in the system trusted it, because every floor — a request’s minimum_isolation, the daemon’s SANDBOX_MIN_ISOLATION, placement among daemons — compares against the tier the provider reports, and the provider reported vm. Underneath the label sat WSL, whose security model opens with Microsoft’s own sentence: “WSL provides a Linux environment that is deeply integrated with Windows. It is not a security sandbox for running untrusted code.”

    v0.27.2, released this morning, changes the label. The wslc per-run mode now reports container by default, so a vm or kernel floor “refuses it before anything runs, marked not dispatched with the reason isolation” — and a daemon started with SANDBOX_MIN_ISOLATION=vm or kernel refuses to start at all until the operator sets the opt-in. An operator who accepts Microsoft’s statement can set SANDBOX_WSLC_ACCEPT_VM_TIER=1, and the mode reports vm again — with that statement attached. Where a caller reads it: Describe carries the qualification as isolation_qualification, and so do the daemon’s startup log and CLI banner; plimsoll’s own doc is explicit that no run record and no run request carries it, because a record states the provider’s name and the tier alone.

    What was missing was never the mechanism. The per-run mode gives each run a genuine Hyper-V VM: a fresh kernel, its own dockerd and disk, deleted after the run. What was missing was a vendor willing to vouch for the boundary, and plimsoll’s hardened mode will not: it names four grounds for refusing this provider, Microsoft’s sentence only the first (the VMs share parts of Windows, like the graphics card, with what runs inside them; five of the controls the docker provider applies are missing inside each VM; the whole path rests on a wslc.exe command Microsoft has not documented). A tier is a trust statement before it is a mechanism, which is why a real Hyper-V VM per run was not enough to be vm.

    The acceptance also leaves a paper trail, narrower than it first sounds, and the narrowing is the honest part. A run record is the daemon’s statement of what it ran and where, so a request refused before dispatch — having run nothing — writes no record; its receipt is the not-dispatched error marked isolation. (Plimsoll has one other door: a session call that may have run but got no answer can leave a record marked unanswered; wslc does not support sessions, so on this provider a record speaks only for runs that ran.) And on the question the label was supposed to answer, the record carries the provider’s name and the tier, with gVisor on also the policy gvisor:proven, and nothing else about the wall — the rest of its fields, digests and timestamps and environment, are evidence about the run, not more truth about the isolation. “A run record does not name the daemon’s release,” the notes say, “so a record from v0.27.0 or v0.27.1 that names wslc and vm was made without the setting; from v0.27.2 on, such a record shows the operator set it.” On its own a record cannot close that inference — it takes the deployment’s own knowledge of which release ran — but with the version known, the eras read differently: before 0.27.2 a wslc record reporting vm was minted with nobody accepting anything, and from 0.27.2 on it could only exist because the acceptance setting (1 or true) was enabled on that daemon. That is the same shape CrewAI’s refusal ended on, where running untrusted code without a boundary became an explicit unsafe_mode=True someone sets on purpose — with one difference worth stealing: CrewAI’s flag is a constructor argument that leaves no trace where it was used, and this acceptance is pinned to a daemon’s configuration, where an audit can find it.

    In October I ran plimsoll’s floor against its wasm provider — the same floor mechanism, a demand for the vm tier from a process-tier backend refused in under a millisecond before the snippet executed — and wrote that a tier label is only worth what the honest paragraph under it says. Nothing here runs on Windows, so the wslc refusal is the release’s word, not a run of mine. But the release welds the paragraph onto the label: a caller asking the daemon what it is now gets Microsoft’s sentence in the same answer as the tier, and a wslc record reporting vm is, on a known release, evidence that the daemon was configured to accept it — a fact about configuration, not about whether a human read the sentence before setting it. The caveat stopped living in the docs where nobody on the request path re-reads it.

  • Nov 17, 2026

    A build that outlasts OpenCode’s foreground shell timeout used to be killed in release builds. In 2.3.1, it carries on in the background and reports back when it finishes. That saves long builds. It also changes what a retry does: a wrapper that treats the expired wait as a stopped command can start a second copy against the same checkout.

    The tagged shell tool, which I checked without running OpenCode, returns a shellID while the command is still running, an output-file path and a null exitCode. Its notice tells the model: “Do not start another copy while it is running.” A client consuming that result needs to keep the handle and the running state through to completion or confirmed cancellation before retrying.

    There are now two meanings for the timeout field. For an ordinary foreground shell call, timeout: 0 selects the default 120 seconds; a positive value sets how long to wait before backgrounding. For an explicitly backgrounded command, a positive timeout still stops the command. The change also removes experimental.shell_timeout_background: old configs containing it keep loading, but the key is dropped. A saved false no longer buys the old kill-on-timeout behavior.
